title: Vishvamitra and the prayer for a stirred mind
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hook: a king loses to a sage's staff, and the Gayatri asks for one thing
carry: the gayatri asks one thing: stir our minds
tomorrow: the Gayatri's first word points. at what, exactly?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Isha ended on a request, lead us by the good path, and a line: what the mind keeps remembering, it holds at the end. Today, a verse this path already knows by sound, read the way a reader reads.

Ten past six, a kitchen in New Jersey, the kettle not on yet. Nani stands at the window with her eyes half shut, saying the same three short lines she says every morning. Priya leans in the doorway in a hoodie, holding a printout. The school's winter assembly wants each senior to share one line from their own tradition, and Priya has written GAYATRI at the top and nothing under it. She waits for Nani to finish. Then: Nani, where's the verb? Nani smiles. There are two, she says. One is ours. One is his.
screen: `TEN PAST SIX. THE KETTLE ISN'T ON.`
`WHERE'S THE VERB?` → `TWO. ONE IS OURS. ONE IS HIS.`

segments.voice: Nani's answer starts with a story, because this verse has a seer, and tradition names him Vishvamitra. Before he was a sage, he was a king. In the Ramayana, King Vishvamitra rides with his army into the forest home of the sage Vasishtha, and the sage feeds every soldier from one wish-granting cow. The king wants her. He offers a hundred thousand cows. Vasishtha says no. So the king takes her by force, and loses: the cow calls up warriors of her own, and when Vishvamitra throws every weapon he has, Vasishtha's plain wooden staff swallows them all. The king stands there with nothing and says, more or less: shame on a warrior's strength; a sage's power is the real power. He walks away from his throne to find it. Now the verse he's remembered for. Tat savitur varenyam, bhargo devasya dhimahi, dhiyo yo nah prachodayat. Find the verbs. Dhimahi: we hold in mind. Prachodayat: may he stir. In plain English: we hold in mind that radiance of the god Savitr, worth choosing; may he stir our thoughts. And here's the teaching. The Gayatri doesn't ask for rain, or wealth, or victory. It asks that the mind be moved by a light beyond it. That's why so many Hindus say it at dawn and dusk, and why many families give it to a child first, at the sacred-thread ceremony. Of everything a person could ask for, the tradition puts this one first.
screen: `A KING LOSES TO A SAGE'S STAFF.` · `DHIMAHI: WE HOLD IN MIND.` · `PRACHODAYAT: MAY HE STIR.` · `NOT RAIN, NOT WEALTH, NOT VICTORY.` · then, large: `IT ASKS FOR A MIND MOVED.`

segments.voice: On any scrap of paper, write the two verbs far apart: dhimahi on the left, prachodayat on the right. Under the first write we hold in mind, under the second may our thoughts be stirred, and draw one line joining them. Then rest your eyes on the page while the time runs.
The Gayatri and the peace chants, read word by word. Today, the map: two verbs, and a king who learned what's worth asking for.
screen: `THE GAYATRI AND THE PEACE CHANTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the Gayatri asks one thing: stir our minds. A king gave up a throne to learn that, and of everything Nani could ask for at ten past six, it's the one she asks first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus say the Gayatri at dawn and dusk, and in many families it is taught at the sacred-thread ceremony; traditions differ on who chants it, some keeping it for those who have received the thread and others teaching it to all. Tradition names Vishvamitra as its seer.

Gayatri.meaning: a Rig Veda verse said at dawn, named for its meter

dhimahi.meaning: we hold in mind, or we meditate on

prachodayat.meaning: may he stir, may he urge on

Vishvamitra.meaning: a king who became a great sage; tradition names him the Gayatri's seer

Vasishtha.meaning: a great sage of the Vedas and the Ramayana

notes: Days 1499–1510 share this title. The Gayatri runs 1499–1506 (1499 the map, 1500 tat, 1501 savitur, 1502 varenyam, 1503 bhargo devasya, 1504 dhimahi, 1505 dhiyo yo nah, 1506 prachodayat); the peace chants run 1507–1510 (1507 saha navavatu and the dual, 1508 sound or sense, 1509 Yajurveda 36.17, 1510 Rig Veda 10.191). Earlier Gayatri days (108, 1262–1267) covered its source, Savitr's hymns, the meter, the vyahritis and the Brihadaranyaka reading; this run reads the grammar. Days 1769–1776 cover the Upanishads' peace chants by meaning; 1507–1510 avoid those angles.

As on day 108, the Gayatri is spoken in full in transliteration. Traditions differ on who may chant it (upanayana); the practice writes the verbs and English rather than chanting, and howItsDone names both views. A Keeper must decide whether the full Sanskrit should be spoken in the app.

'dhimahi' rendered 'we meditate on, or may we hold in mind' because translators differ (some read it from dha, 'may we attain'). Confirm. 'Doesn't ask for rain, or wealth, or a long life' describes the verse's content only.
Gloss 'Gayatri: named for its meter' follows day 108; confirm.
